inline_comments.comment: `startTime` is captured before the `options.presets.apply()` and `indexGenerator.getIndex()` awaits, meaning time spent fetching the story index and warming up requests counts against the 30-second module-graph timeout. If fetching the index takes 20 seconds on a slow machine, the polling interval only has 10 seconds to observe a non-empty `fileToModulesMap` before a spurious timeout fires. `startTime` should be captured after the warm-up phase completes — i.e., just before the `setInterval` call on line 137.
Commented-out debug log left in: `// logger.info(\`Story ${entry.id} absolute path: ${absolutePath}\`);`. This should be removed before merging.

After a `ChangeDetectionFailureError`, `resolveReadiness({status:'error'})` is called and `this.readinessResolved` is set to `true`, but `dispose()` is NOT called, so scanning continues. If a subsequent scan succeeds, `resolveReadiness({status:'ready'})` is a no-op because `readinessResolved` is already `true`. This means `getChangeDetectionReadiness()` is permanently stuck at `{status:'error'}` even after the service fully recovers. Consumers using `getChangeDetectionReadiness()` to gate UI behavior will never see the service transition back to `ready`. Consider either resetting `readinessResolved` on success, or splitting the concept into a startup probe vs. a live-state signal.

`Math.min(...Array.from(affectedStoryFiles.values(), ...))` spreads all distance values as individual function arguments. JavaScript engines typically impose a call-stack argument limit (V8 uses ~65,535). For a pathological module graph where one changed file reaches a very large number of story files this will throw a `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. Prefer a reduce: `Array.from(affectedStoryFiles.values()).reduce((min, { distance }) => Math.min(min, distance), Infinity)`.

`buildStatuses` fires `getChangedFiles()` and `getRepoRoot()` in the same `Promise.all`. Because `getChangedFiles()` internally `await`s `getRepoRoot()` before running the diff commands, on the very first invocation (before `this.repoRoot` is cached) both calls race to call `execa('git', ['rev-parse', '--show-toplevel'])` concurrently, spawning two subprocesses when one would suffice. You can remove the standalone `getRepoRoot()` call from `Promise.all` and derive the repo root from the `GitDiffResult` instead, or await `getRepoRoot()` first before starting the parallel work.

When a shorter path to an already-visited node is discovered (`previousDistance > distance`), the node is re-enqueued via `queue.push({ node: importer, distance })`. However, the previous entry (with the longer, stale distance) is still in the queue and will later be dequeued and processed, causing redundant traversal of its subtree. Because all edge weights are 1, a standard BFS that visits each `ModuleNode` exactly once on first encounter (discarding re-encounters) would always produce correct shortest distances without the redundant work. The stale entries are ultimately harmless due to the `previousDistance <= distance` guard, but they add unnecessary overhead on graphs with many convergent paths.

The test "prefers modified over affected when the same story is reached by multiple changed files" doesn't actually exercise the `mergeStatusValues` 'modified beats affected' case. Both `src/direct.ts` and `src/indirect.ts` each reach only one story file (`Button.stories.tsx`), so for each changed file independently that story file is always at `lowestDistance` and is always assigned `'status-value:modified'`. The merge of `('modified', 'modified')` trivially returns `'modified'` — the priority logic in `mergeStatusValues` is not exercised. To properly test the intent, the scenario needs at least two story files so that one changed file assigns `modified` to the nearer story and `affected` to the farther one.

`ChangeDetectionService` is exported directly from `'./change-detection/service'`, bypassing the barrel (`'./change-detection/index.ts'`) that already re-exports it. The two exports adjacent to each other — one using the barrel for readiness types, one going straight to the implementation file — are inconsistent. Prefer `from './change-detection'` for both to keep consumers insulated from internal file layout.

general_comments.comment: `readiness.ts` uses module-level mutable singletons (`readinessDeferred`, `readinessState`) that are reset by `ChangeDetectionService`'s constructor via `resetChangeDetectionReadiness()`. If a consumer calls `getChangeDetectionReadiness()` before the `ChangeDetectionService` constructor runs (receiving the old `readinessDeferred.promise`), and the constructor then resets the deferred, that consumer's promise is silently orphaned and will never settle. More broadly, hiding a global side-effect inside a constructor is unexpected: callers can't reason about it without reading the implementation. Consider moving the reset to an explicit `initialize()` method or injecting a readiness resolver as a constructor parameter so the lifetime is visible at the call site.

`getStoryIdsByAbsolutePath` in `service.ts` silently skips all entries where `entry.type !== 'story'`, which includes MDX `docs` entries. If a docs file is modified, no change-detection status will be surfaced even if the file is tracked by git and appears in the module graph. This may be intentional (docs changes might not need a 'modified' badge), but there is no comment explaining the decision. At minimum, a brief note would prevent future contributors from assuming docs support is simply missing and adding it incorrectly.
